guides.title: Cold & Hypothermia
guides.summary: Layering, frostbite, hypothermia and staying warm.

sections.heading: Spot hypothermia
sections.body: Watch for the 'umbles' — stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles — plus shivering and confusion. Treat mild cases with dry insulation, shelter from wind, warm sweet drinks, and gentle movement — not a hot bath. Warm the core first; handle the person gently.

sections.heading: Frostbite
sections.body: Do not rub frostbitten skin, and do not thaw it if it might refreeze — refreezing causes far worse damage. Rewarm in water at body temperature (about 37–39 °C / 99–102 °F), never over direct heat. Warm nipped fingers or toes against your own belly or armpits.

sections.heading: Layer for cold
sections.body: Wear a wicking base, an insulating mid, and a wind/waterproof shell, and adjust to avoid sweating — wet layers freeze you. Cotton kills in the cold: once wet it stops insulating, so choose wool or synthetics. Cover your head and neck.

sections.heading: Stay warm
sections.body: Windchill is the real killer — get out of the wind. Eat and drink often; your body burns fuel fast to make heat. Vent before you sweat, keep spare batteries and lighters warm in an inner pocket, and change into dry socks before sleeping.

sections.heading: How Your Body Loses Heat: The Physics of Cold Exposure
sections.body:
Core body temperature is regulated within about half a degree of 37°C (98.6°F), and every cold-weather strategy in this guide is really an attempt to slow one or more of five physical heat-loss pathways: radiation, conduction, convection, evaporation, and respiration. At rest in still, moderate air, radiation — heat leaving your body as infrared energy, mostly from uncovered skin and the head — accounts for over half of total heat loss, which is why a hat matters more than its small surface area suggests. Conduction is direct heat transfer into whatever you're touching; because water conducts heat roughly 25 times faster than still air, sitting on cold ground or wearing wet clothing drains core heat far faster than dry air at the same temperature ever could. Convection is heat carried away by moving air or water — it's what wind chill actually measures — and it works by continuously stripping away the thin layer of air your body has warmed against your skin, forcing you to keep reheating a new layer.

Evaporation cools you whenever moisture leaves your skin or lungs, which is why sweating inside a cold-weather layering system is dangerous rather than merely uncomfortable: the same evaporative cooling that protects you from overheating in summer will pull heat out of you in winter the moment you stop moving. Respiration loses both heat and moisture with every breath, which is one reason caloric and fluid needs climb in cold, dry air. Shivering is your body's emergency response — involuntary muscle contraction that can raise metabolic heat production two to five times above resting levels — but it is inefficient and unsustainable, a stopgap while you add insulation, get moving, or find shelter, not a substitute for any of those.

sections.heading: Reading Wind Chill: Why the Thermometer Lies to You
sections.body:
Air temperature alone tells you almost nothing about how fast exposed skin will lose heat once wind is added, because moving air continuously strips away the thin boundary layer your body has warmed. The U.S. National Weather Service and Environment Canada both use a wind chill formula — WCT(°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75·V^0.16 + 0.4275·T·V^0.16, with T in °F and V in mph — that converts an air temperature and wind speed into an equivalent 'feels like' number based on how fast a model of exposed facial skin cools. The effect is dramatic and non-linear: air at 20°F (−7°C) with a 20 mph wind produces a wind chill of about −9°F (−23°C), and at that wind chill, frostbite can develop on exposed skin in as little as 30 minutes rather than the hours it would take in calm air at the actual temperature.

Two details are easy to misunderstand. First, wind chill is a skin-exposure metric, not a measure of how fast inanimate objects (a car engine, a water bottle) cool — those follow ordinary physics based on actual air temperature, not the wind chill number. Second, the formula assumes a walking pace generates some of the wind itself, so standing still in calm air but moving briskly can create a self-generated wind chill worth accounting for. Wind chill charts, readily available from national weather services, convert the formula into a lookup table by temperature and wind speed and are worth checking before any extended cold-weather outing, not just the forecast high and low.

sections.heading: Cold-Water Immersion and the 1-10-1 Rule
sections.body:
Falling into cold water is a different — and faster — emergency than dry cold exposure, and it kills through a predictable sequence best remembered as the 1-10-1 rule. In the first 1 minute, cold shock triggers an involuntary gasp reflex and hyperventilation that can cause immediate drowning if your face is underwater, plus a spike in heart rate and blood pressure that is dangerous for anyone with cardiovascular risk; the only strategy is to get your breathing under control and avoid inhaling water. Over the next roughly 10 minutes, you have useful, coordinated muscle function — this is your window to self-rescue, get out of the water, or get a flotation device on, because cold rapidly degrades fine motor control and swimming ability long before hypothermia itself sets in; most cold-water drownings happen from swim failure in this window, not from hypothermia. True hypothermia — the drop in core temperature that causes confusion and eventual unconsciousness — typically takes on the order of 1 hour or more depending on water temperature, insulation, and body size, which means many immersion victims have far more survivable time than they assume if they stop struggling and focus on conserving heat.

If you can't get out of the water, adopt the Heat Escape Lessening Posture (HELP): draw your knees to your chest and your arms tight across them to protect the torso and groin, the areas of fastest heat loss. In a group, huddle chest-to-chest to share warmth. Keep clothing on rather than removing it — trapped water inside clothing still insulates once it warms slightly against your skin — and climb as far out of the water as possible onto any floating object, since heat loss into water is far faster than into cold air.

sections.heading: Non-Freezing Cold Injuries: Trench Foot and Chilblains
sections.body:
Not every cold injury involves tissue actually freezing. Trench foot (also called immersion foot) develops after feet are kept wet and cold — typically 32–50°F (0–10°C) — for extended periods, commonly many hours to days, without ever dropping below freezing; sustained vasoconstriction starves the tissue of oxygen and damages small blood vessels and nerves, producing numbness, swelling, blotchy red-to-blue skin, and in severe cases blistering and tissue death. It earned its name in World War I trench warfare, where soldiers stood in cold water for days, but it's a real risk for anyone in wet boots or socks in cold conditions — hikers, hunters, and anyone whose footwear fails to keep water out. Prevention is straightforward and almost entirely about moisture management: change out of wet socks as soon as practical, dry feet thoroughly at rest breaks, and rotate multiple pairs of socks so a dry pair is always available.

Chilblains (pernio) are a distinct, usually milder injury caused by repeated exposure to cold, damp air — not immersion — that triggers small, itchy or painful red-to-purple bumps, most often on fingers, toes, ears, and the nose. The leading theory is that rapid rewarming of blood vessels that have been constricted by cold causes fluid to leak from capillaries into surrounding tissue, producing localized inflammation. Both conditions are treated the same cautious way: gradual rewarming at room temperature, not hot water or direct heat sources, since heat applied to numbed or damaged tissue risks burns the person can't feel; the area should never be rubbed or massaged, and any blistering or skin breakdown should be treated as a wound and monitored for infection.

sections.heading: Fueling the Furnace: Nutrition and Hydration in the Cold
sections.body:
Cold exposure is metabolically expensive. Shivering alone can raise resting energy expenditure several-fold, and combined with the extra physical effort of moving through snow, breaking trail, or simply wearing many pounds of extra clothing, sustained cold-weather activity can push daily caloric needs to 4,000–6,000 kcal, roughly double an ordinary day's requirement. Fat is the most calorie-dense macronutrient at about 9 kcal per gram (versus roughly 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrate and protein) and digests slowly, making high-fat foods — nuts, cheese, fatty meats, chocolate — disproportionately useful for sustained cold-weather energy, while simple carbohydrates are better reserved for a fast pre-exertion boost.

Hydration is the more commonly overlooked half of this equation, because thirst is a poor signal in the cold: a phenomenon called cold-induced diuresis causes the body to shed fluid through increased urination as blood is shunted away from the skin toward the core, and dry, cold air increases water loss through every breath you exhale. The net effect is that people dehydrate in winter conditions without ever feeling thirsty, and dehydration itself worsens cold tolerance by reducing blood volume available to carry heat to the extremities. The fix is deliberate, scheduled fluid intake regardless of thirst, favoring warm — not scalding — drinks, and avoiding alcohol, which causes peripheral vasodilation, a warm, flushed feeling on the skin that is actually your body dumping core heat faster, one of the more dangerous cold-weather misconceptions.

sections.heading: Building Emergency Shelter and Fire in Snow
sections.body:
Snow is, counterintuitively, an excellent insulator because it's mostly trapped air; a properly built snow shelter — a snow cave dug into a deep drift, or a quinzhee mounded up and hollowed out — can hold an interior temperature near 32°F (0°C) even when the outside air is far colder, simply by blocking wind and radiant heat loss to the night sky. The most important design detail is a raised sleeping platform above the level of the entrance: cold air sinks, so a shelter dug with a lower 'cold trap' near the door and a raised sleeping shelf traps the coldest air away from your body. A small ventilation hole poked through the roof with a stick is not optional — without it, carbon dioxide (and carbon monoxide if any flame or stove is used inside) can build up to dangerous levels in a sealed snow shelter.

Starting a fire in wet or snowy conditions requires carrying reliable dry tinder rather than hoping to find it — cotton balls soaked in petroleum jelly, dryer lint, or commercial fire-starter cubes kept in a waterproof container are standard choices. When gathering fuel on site, look for 'squaw wood' — small dead branches still attached to standing trees, which stay drier than anything lying on wet ground — and shave curls into it with a knife to expose dry inner wood as feather sticks. Build the fire on a platform of green logs or bark laid on top of the snow; without one, a fire's own heat melts the snow beneath it and the fire slowly sinks into a self-dug pit of meltwater and extinguishes itself.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body: None of the techniques above matter if the gear underneath them fails; here's the practical shopping list for genuine cold-weather readiness.
ingredients: Insulated, waterproof boots with removable liners, sized to allow a thick sock without cutting off circulation, from an outdoor/camping retailer
Wool or synthetic base-layer thermal underwear (top and bottom) — avoid cotton, which loses nearly all insulating value when wet
A sleeping bag rated at least 10-15°F below the coldest temperature you expect to encounter, from an outdoor/camping retailer
A closed-cell foam sleeping pad, ideally paired with an inflatable pad, for insulation from the cold ground
Chemical hand and toe warmers (air-activated iron-oxide packets), sold individually or by the box at any outdoor or hardware store
A stove rated for cold weather — standard butane/isobutane canister stoves lose pressure below freezing; a white-gas or cold-weather-blend canister stove performs more reliably
A wind- and waterproof hard-shell outer jacket and pants
A wide-mouth, insulated water bottle or vacuum flask (a narrow-mouth bottle's cap can freeze shut)
A fire-starting kit: waterproof or strike-anywhere matches, or a ferrocerium rod, plus manufactured tinder such as petroleum-jelly cotton balls
A basic first-aid kit with supplies suited to blisters and skin injuries, from a pharmacy
A compact outdoor thermometer to track actual ambient temperature rather than guessing
An avalanche beacon, collapsible shovel, and probe if traveling in snow-covered mountain terrain, from a mountaineering/outdoor retailer

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Running a Cold-Weather Readiness Drill
sections.body: The best time to learn how your gear and body actually perform in the cold is on a low-stakes practice day, not in a real emergency — here's how to run that drill safely.
steps: Choose a genuinely cold, dry day (air temperature at or below 32°F/0°C) and run this drill somewhere you can retreat indoors within a few minutes, such as a backyard or nearby park — never make your first cold-weather test in remote terrain.
Before heading out, check both the air temperature and wind speed and calculate (or look up) the wind chill, then compare your instinctive sense of how cold it'll feel against the real number.

Dress in your complete planned layering system, then stand still outdoors for about 15 minutes, paying attention to which body parts — fingers, toes, ears, nose — cool first; these are the zones to reinforce with better gear.

Do 10 minutes of easy exertion, such as a brisk walk or carrying a loaded pack, and notice how quickly you begin sweating under your layers — a system that makes you sweat during light activity will chill you dangerously once you stop.
Practice shedding your outer shell layer at the first sign of overheating, and time yourself doing it with gloves on; it should take well under a minute.
If snow is available, spend 15-20 minutes practicing a simple wind block or the start of a snow shelter, timing the effort so you know what it actually costs in a real situation.

With someone else present and water or snow on hand to extinguish it, practice starting a fire using only a ferro rod and tinder or dead-standing wood gathered on site — do this before you ever need it for real.
Set a sealed bottle of water outside in the shade for the duration of the drill and check how much it has cooled by the end, as a concrete illustration of how fast exposed water freezes.
Afterward, debrief with yourself or your group: which gear item did you reach for most, which one underperformed, and what would you change before the next outing.

Only repeat the drill on a colder or windier day once you've comfortably handled a calmer one — cold tolerance and gear confidence should be built incrementally, and any numbness beyond mild tingling is the signal to stop and rewarm immediately.

guides.title: Heat & Desert
guides.summary: Beating heat exhaustion, sun and desert travel.

sections.heading: Travel cool, rest hot
sections.body: In the desert, travel at dawn, dusk, or night and rest in shade during the peak heat — a still body needs far less water. Sand is coldest and firmest to walk on at night.

sections.heading: Cover up
sections.body: Stay covered in loose, light clothing; it shades you and slows sweat loss. Keep your mouth shut and breathe through your nose to cut moisture loss. Wet a cloth and drape it on your neck and wrists to cool the blood near the surface.

sections.heading: Heat illness
sections.body: Heat exhaustion — heavy sweat, weakness, nausea — means stop, get in shade, and sip water now. Heat stroke (hot red skin, confusion, and no sweat) is a life-threatening emergency: cool the body fast by any means and get help.

sections.heading: Water & salt
sections.body: Ration sweat, not water: work in the cool hours and drink when thirsty. Replace salt with food or a pinch in water, or cramps and worse follow. Do not lie directly on hot sand or rock — put insulation between you and the ground.

sections.heading: How the Body Sheds Heat: Thermoregulation Explained
sections.body:
In hot conditions, evaporative cooling from sweat is by far the body's most powerful heat-dumping mechanism: evaporating one liter of sweat carries away roughly 580 kilocalories of heat, drawn from the latent heat of vaporization of water. Alongside sweating, the body vasodilates — widening blood vessels near the skin — to move warm blood from the core to the surface where it can radiate and convect heat away, which is why skin flushes and pulse rises in heat even before you feel especially hot; this redirection of blood flow is also why cardiac output and heart rate climb substantially during heat stress even without exercise. A well-acclimatized, fit person doing sustained heavy exertion in heat can sweat 1-2 liters per hour, with a practical sustainable upper limit for gut absorption and replacement around 2-3 liters per hour — beyond that, the body simply cannot take in fluid fast enough to keep pace with losses.

The critical limitation is that evaporation only works when the surrounding air can actually accept more water vapor — sweat has to evaporate, not just appear, to cool you. This is governed by the vapor pressure gradient between your wet skin and the surrounding air, which is why high humidity is often more dangerous than high temperature alone: at high relative humidity, air is already close to saturated, sweat can bead and drip without evaporating, and your primary cooling system effectively stops working even though you may be sweating profusely. This is the physiological reason heat index and wet-bulb temperature matter more for real risk than the number on a dry thermometer.

sections.heading: Wet-Bulb Temperature: The Real Limit of Human Heat Survival
sections.body:
Wet-bulb temperature is measured with a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in a wet wick and exposed to airflow; because evaporation cools the wick, the reading is always at or below the actual (dry-bulb) air temperature, and the gap between the two shrinks as humidity rises — at 100% relative humidity, wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperature are identical, because no further evaporation is possible. Wet-bulb temperature is a useful single number because it captures both heat and humidity together, unlike the heat index used in most U.S. weather forecasts, which is an empirical approximation calibrated around a baseline humidity and doesn't correspond directly to a physical wet-bulb measurement.

Physiologically, skin temperature sits around 35°C (95°F); researchers have long cited a wet-bulb temperature of 35°C as a theoretical upper survivability limit, because at or above that point there is no longer any vapor pressure gradient between skin and air, evaporative cooling stops working entirely, and even a resting, unclothed, well-hydrated person in the shade with unlimited water will fatally overheat within hours purely from metabolic heat with nowhere to go. More recent human-subject research suggests the real-world critical threshold is likely lower, closer to a 30-31°C wet-bulb temperature, especially for people who are older, less fit, or engaged in any physical activity. Wet-bulb readings approaching this range have already been recorded in parts of the Persian Gulf and South Asia during extreme heat events, and climate projections indicate such conditions will become more frequent and geographically widespread — this is the scientific basis behind warnings that some regions may become periodically uninhabitable without air conditioning.

sections.heading: Finding and Purifying Water When Stranded in the Desert
sections.body:
If you're genuinely stranded without a reliable water source, the single most important rule is the opposite of instinct: never ration your water intake to make a small supply last longer. Dehydration degrades judgment, coordination, and the body's own cooling ability faster than a small water deficit ever saves you — the correct response to a limited supply is to ration exertion, travel only during cooler hours, and seek shade, not to ration drinking. To find water, look for converging trails, which often lead animals to a water source, and for patches of green vegetation such as cottonwood or willow trees, which typically indicate a shallow water table even where the surface looks bone-dry. In a dry wash or arroyo, the outside of a bend is usually where water collects closest to the surface — digging a shallow pit there, even in seemingly dry sand, can reach damp or wet soil worth straining and treating.

A solar still — a plastic sheet stretched over a pit dug in damp ground, weighted in the center over a collection container — can extract a small amount of water through condensation, typically well under a liter per day, so it's a supplement to a survival situation rather than a primary strategy. Any water gathered this way, from a still, seep, or pool, should be purified before drinking: boiling for at least one minute (three minutes above roughly 6,500 feet/2,000 m elevation, where water boils at a lower temperature) kills essentially all pathogens, and purification tablets or a portable filter are reliable backups. Purification removes biological contamination but not dissolved minerals or salts — stagnant desert pools in alkaline or gypsum-rich soil can be too mineral-laden to drink safely even after proper purification, and should be avoided if any alternative exists.

sections.heading: Sunburn and UV Overexposure: Recognition and Treatment
sections.body:
Sunburn is direct tissue damage from ultraviolet radiation — mostly UVB, with UVA contributing to deeper damage and long-term skin aging — that triggers an inflammatory response as the skin repairs DNA damage in its cells. The reaction is delayed: peak redness, pain, and swelling typically appear 12-24 hours after exposure, well after the sun exposure that caused it, which is why feeling fine at the time is an unreliable guide during the exposure itself. The UV Index, published in most weather forecasts on a scale that commonly runs from 0 to 11+, is a better real-time guide than how hot or bright the day feels; UV intensity is typically highest within a few hours of solar noon (roughly 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.) regardless of air temperature, and is intensified by high altitude, reflective surfaces like sand, water, and snow, and thin cloud cover, which blocks little UV despite feeling cooler.

Sunscreen SPF ratings describe UVB blocking: SPF 30 filters out about 97% of UVB radiation and SPF 50 about 98% — the difference between high SPF numbers is smaller than it sounds, and no sunscreen blocks 100%. Reapplication every two hours, and immediately after swimming or heavy sweating, matters more than chasing a higher SPF number. For a burn that has already happened, treatment is cooling (cool — not ice-cold — compresses or a bath), hydration, aloe vera gel, and an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen for pain and swelling; a burn with significant blistering is a second-degree burn requiring more careful wound care and should be watched for signs of infection. Cumulative lifetime UV exposure, including repeated sunburns, is the primary modifiable risk factor for skin cancer, making sun protection a long-term health habit, not just a same-day comfort issue.

sections.heading: Vehicle Breakdown in the Desert: What Actually to Do
sections.body:
The near-universal advice from search-and-rescue professionals is to stay with your vehicle if it breaks down in a remote desert area, unless you know with certainty that help is a short, safe walk away — a vehicle is far easier for searchers to spot from the ground or air than a walking person, and it provides shade, shelter, and a fixed point that matches where you told someone you'd be. Use the shade cast by the vehicle rather than the interior, and stay a foot or two clear of the metal body itself, which can reach 140-160°F (60-70°C) or more in direct desert sun and will burn exposed skin on contact; the strip of shade that moves around the vehicle through the day is often the coolest available spot, especially if you dig a shallow trench into the slightly cooler subsurface soil beneath it.

Make the vehicle as visible as possible: raise the hood (a widely recognized distress signal), tie a brightly colored cloth to the antenna or side mirror, and use anything reflective — a signal mirror, a phone screen, even a shard of glass — to flash sunlight toward passing aircraft or distant roads, aiming carefully since a well-aimed flash is visible for miles. Signals in groups of three (three flashes, three fires, three blasts of a horn) are the internationally recognized distress pattern. One persistent myth worth retiring: radiator fluid and coolant are not an emergency water source — they contain ethylene glycol, which is toxic, and should never be consumed regardless of how it's diluted. Conserve the vehicle's battery for the horn, lights, or hazards rather than running the engine or accessories continuously.

sections.heading: Heat Acclimatization: Training Your Body Ahead of Time
sections.body:
Heat tolerance is a real, measurable physiological adaptation, not just willpower, and it develops predictably with repeated heat exposure over roughly 7 to 14 days. The core adaptations include an expansion of blood plasma volume, which lets the cardiovascular system deliver more blood to the skin for cooling without straining the heart as much; sweating that begins earlier and at a lower body temperature, so cooling starts before core temperature climbs as high; and sweat that becomes progressively more dilute, containing less sodium, which conserves electrolytes during long heat exposure. Together, these changes measurably lower heart rate and core temperature for the same workload in heat compared to an unacclimatized person doing identical work.

Acclimatization is built through progressively longer periods of heat exposure combined with mild-to-moderate exertion — for example, 60-100 minutes of light activity in the heat, repeated daily, gradually increasing duration or intensity as tolerance builds — rather than through passive sitting in the heat, which produces little adaptation. It is also partially and gradually reversible: most of the benefit fades within roughly 2-3 weeks of returning to cooler conditions, which is why people who travel from a mild climate to a hot one, or whose first genuinely hot day arrives after a mild spring, are disproportionately represented in early-season heat illness cases. Anyone planning sustained work or exertion in a hot climate — a desert hike, outdoor labor, a summer athletic season — benefits measurably from a deliberate one-to-two week acclimatization period rather than starting at full intensity on day one.

sections.heading: Desert Heat Myths Worth Unlearning
sections.body:
Several widely repeated pieces of desert survival advice are wrong in ways that can be dangerous. Chewing on a barrel cactus or other cactus flesh for emergency water is a persistent myth traceable partly to old films; in reality, most barrel cactus flesh is acidic and contains alkaloids that commonly cause vomiting and diarrhea — a net water loss in an emergency, not a gain — and it should not be relied on as a water source. Rationing water to 'make it last' is another dangerous habit: dehydration degrades your capacity to think clearly and to cool yourself well before a small water deficit would have mattered, so the correct move is always to drink to your body's needs and instead conserve water by reducing exertion and heat exposure.

Dark, heavy clothing is sometimes assumed to be simply worse than going shirtless, but the comparison is more nuanced: loose, light-colored, breathable, UPF-rated clothing that covers skin generally outperforms bare skin in direct sun, because it blocks UV radiation and can trap a layer of slightly cooler air near the body while still allowing sweat to evaporate through the fabric — which is the reasoning behind traditional desert dress across many hot-climate cultures, not folklore. Finally, the idea that you'll feel thirsty well before you're seriously dehydrated is unreliable in practice, because thirst perception lags measurable fluid deficit, especially during heavy exertion or for older adults whose thirst response blunts with age — by the time thirst is strong, meaningful dehydration has typically already occurred, which is why scheduled drinking rather than drinking purely to thirst is the standard recommendation for real heat exposure.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body: Surviving and staying comfortable in serious heat depends on a short list of unglamorous, genuinely effective gear.
ingredients: A wide-brimmed hat (at least a 3-inch brim) or a legionnaire-style cap with a neck flap, from an outdoor/camping retailer or general department store
Loose-fitting, light-colored, tightly woven long-sleeve shirt and pants, ideally with a UPF (UV Protection Factor) rating, from an outdoor retailer
Broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen rated SPF 30 or higher, from any pharmacy or supermarket
Wraparound sunglasses rated to block 99-100% of UVA/UVB, from an optics retailer or pharmacy
An oral rehydration or electrolyte-replacement product (powder, tablets, or pre-mixed) with a meaningful sodium content, from a pharmacy or sporting-goods store
At least two separate water containers or a hydration bladder with a combined multi-liter capacity, from an outdoor/camping retailer
A lightweight reflective emergency (mylar) blanket, which doubles as a rough signaling surface, from an outdoor retailer
A small dedicated signal mirror, or any compact handheld mirror, from a hardware or outdoor store
A bandana, cooling towel, or similar cloth that can be wetted and worn around the neck for evaporative cooling
Water purification tablets or a compact portable filter, from an outdoor/camping retailer
A basic first-aid kit that includes an aloe-vera or burn gel for sunburn, from a pharmacy
A small, non-mercury thermometer to check actual ambient or shade temperature rather than guessing, from a hardware or general retailer

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Running a Heat-Safety Drill
sections.body: Like cold tolerance, heat safety is a set of skills and personal calibrations best learned on a controlled practice day, not during a real emergency.
steps: Choose a genuinely hot day (85°F/29°C or above) and run this drill somewhere you can retreat to shade or air conditioning within a couple of minutes, such as a backyard or local park, not remote terrain.
Before heading out, check both the temperature and the humidity or heat index and note them together — this trains you to read combined heat risk rather than just the thermometer.
Fill and note the volume of your water container, then walk at a normal pace in full sun for 20-30 minutes wearing your planned heat-weather clothing.

On returning, note how much water you actually drank versus how depleted you feel, and if practical, weigh yourself before and after in similar clothing to get a rough sense of your personal sweat rate.
Deliberately stand in full sun for two minutes, then move into shade and notice the perceived difference — this calibrates how much shade alone is worth seeking during a real exertion.

Practice basic self-checks for dehydration on yourself now — skin turgor (pinch the back of your hand and see how fast it flattens), urine color, and how you subjectively feel — so you recognize your own baseline before it becomes an emergency read.

Mix an electrolyte drink to the label's recommended concentration and taste-test it in advance, rather than for the first time during an actual heat emergency, so you know whether you'll actually drink enough of it.

If you have access to a car, practice popping the hood, tying a bright cloth to the antenna or mirror, and aiming a handheld mirror to flash reflected sunlight at a distant fixed object, to build real skill at signaling.
Debrief afterward: record how much water you needed for that level of heat and exertion, so you can plan quantities more accurately for longer outings.

Build tolerance and testing intensity gradually — repeat later in the hottest part of the afternoon only once you've handled a milder session comfortably, and treat dizziness, nausea, confusion, or the stopping of sweating as an immediate signal to stop, cool down, and seek help.

guides.title: High Altitude: Thin Air, Altitude Illness & Acclimatization
guides.summary: Above roughly 8,000 feet the air itself becomes the hazard — how to read your body's warning signs, pace an ascent, and know exactly when the only correct move is to go back down.

sections.heading: Altitude Is Its Own Climate, Not Just "Cold and Windy"
sections.body: Going up a mountain doesn't just get colder — the air itself thins out in a way that becomes the dominant hazard on its own, independent of temperature. The percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere stays about 21% all the way up, but barometric pressure drops steadily with elevation, so each breath delivers fewer actual oxygen molecules even though the air is chemically the same mix. At sea level, pressure runs around 760 mmHg; by 18,000 feet it has fallen to roughly half that, meaning a lungful of air there carries about half the oxygen molecules of a lungful at the coast, and the body has to work harder for every task from walking to digesting food. Altitude illness becomes a realistic risk above about 8,000 feet (2,400m), rises sharply above 12,000 feet, and above 26,000 feet (8,000m) — the so-called "death zone" — no human body can acclimatize enough to survive indefinitely; the body is slowly deteriorating even at complete rest. Layer on top of the thin air a package of related stresses — intensified UV radiation, low humidity that accelerates dehydration, wide day-to-night temperature swings, and often genuine cold — and altitude qualifies as its own distinct climate to prepare for, not just a colder version of wherever the traveler started from. People routinely underestimate it because the scenery looks like a difficult hike rather than a hostile environment.

sections.heading: How Your Body Responds to Thin Air
sections.body: The body starts adjusting to reduced oxygen within minutes of arrival and keeps adjusting for weeks afterward, on several different timescales at once. Breathing rate and depth increase almost immediately — the hypoxic ventilatory response — and resting heart rate rises to circulate more blood per minute and partially compensate for the lower oxygen content of each breath. Over the following one to three days, the kidneys begin excreting bicarbonate to correct the blood-chemistry disturbance caused by faster, deeper breathing, which is a slower and more durable layer of acclimatization than the immediate cardiovascular response. Over one to two weeks, the body ramps up erythropoietin production and generates more red blood cells to carry more oxygen per liter of blood — the physiological basis of altitude training used by endurance athletes. A practical point for anyone carrying a pulse oximeter: blood oxygen saturation naturally runs lower at altitude even in healthy, well-acclimatized people — readings of 90–94% are commonly normal above 10,000 feet and are not automatically a red flag on their own. A single number matters far less than the trend over hours and days, and especially whether it lines up with how the person actually feels, moves, and thinks — a low reading in someone acting completely normal is a very different situation from the same reading in someone confused or breathless at rest.

sections.heading: Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS): The Common Early Warning
sections.body: AMS is the mild, common end of altitude illness and the warning sign that precedes its dangerous forms — the great majority of people who go too high too fast will experience it in some degree. It typically begins 6 to 12 hours after arriving at an elevation above about 8,000 feet (2,500m), occasionally as late as 24 hours after arrival, which is why symptoms that show up the morning after a fast drive or flight to altitude shouldn't be dismissed as unrelated. The defining symptom is headache, plus at least one of: nausea or loss of appetite, fatigue or unusual weakness, dizziness or lightheadedness, or difficulty sleeping — together it feels a lot like a hangover, minus the drinking, and can be mistaken for simple travel fatigue if no one is watching for it. Mild AMS is managed by stopping the ascent, resting at the current altitude rather than going higher, hydrating, taking ibuprofen or acetaminophen for the headache, and giving the body a day to catch up before continuing. The non-negotiable golden rule is: never ascend to sleep at a higher elevation while AMS symptoms are present — pushing on through symptoms, even mild ones, is the single most common way ordinary AMS turns into HAPE or HACE. If symptoms don't improve, or get worse, despite a full rest day at the same altitude, the correct response shifts decisively from "wait it out" to "go down."

sections.heading: HAPE — High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema
sections.body: HAPE is fluid accumulating in the lungs, driven by altitude-triggered constriction of pulmonary blood vessels that raises pressure in the lung's circulation, and it is a genuine medical emergency rather than a severe case of being out of breath. It most often appears 2 to 4 days after arrival at elevations above roughly 8,000–14,000 feet, and risk climbs noticeably with faster ascent rates, cold exposure, and hard physical exertion soon after arriving at a new altitude. Warning signs: breathlessness that persists at rest, not just on exertion; a dry cough that can progress over hours to pink, frothy sputum; a gurgling or crackling sound in the chest that can sometimes be heard without any equipment simply by listening; extreme, out-of-proportion fatigue on tasks that were easy the day before; and a bluish or gray tinge to lips or fingertips as blood oxygen falls further. Left untreated, HAPE can be fatal within hours, and it can worsen fastest overnight while the person is lying down and less active. The definitive treatment is descent — even a modest drop of 1,000 to 3,000 feet can produce dramatic improvement within a matter of hours. Supplemental oxygen helps significantly if it's available, the person should be kept warm and should not exert themselves further, and if descent must be delayed by terrain or weather, the drug nifedipine can buy time by relaxing the constricted lung vessels. A portable hyperbaric chamber (a Gamow bag) simulates the effect of descent by pressurizing the air around the patient when actual descent isn't immediately possible, but it's a bridge to real descent, never a substitute for it.

sections.heading: HACE — High-Altitude Cerebral Edema
sections.body: HACE is swelling of the brain from altitude exposure and fluid leakage. It's rarer than HAPE but the deadliest form of altitude illness, and it usually develops as a progression from AMS that wasn't respected or acted on in time. The hallmark sign is ataxia — loss of coordination severe enough that the person cannot walk a straight heel-to-toe line and stumbles like they're intoxicated; this single test, having someone try to walk a straight line placing one foot directly in front of the other, is one of the most useful and fastest field checks available at altitude and should be part of any evening camp routine above 10,000 feet. Other signs include a severe headache that doesn't respond to medication, confusion, irrational or uncharacteristic behavior, visual disturbances or hallucinations, and drowsiness that can progress to unresponsiveness and coma. Untreated HACE can kill within roughly 24 hours of the ataxia first appearing. As with HAPE, immediate descent is the definitive treatment — this is not something to wait out until morning or until the next scheduled stop. Dexamethasone can reduce brain swelling and buy critical time, and supplemental oxygen or a Gamow bag can help stabilize someone during evacuation, but neither replaces losing elevation. Never let a person showing HACE symptoms attempt to descend alone; the same impaired coordination and judgment that define the condition make solo descent genuinely dangerous on top of the illness itself, and a companion must physically manage and, if necessary, support the descent with them.

sections.heading: Acclimatization Pacing: The Golden Rules
sections.body: The single biggest risk factor for altitude illness is simply going up too fast, and pacing is the primary defense available before anyone gets sick. The classic strategy is "climb high, sleep low" — hiking to a higher elevation during the day, then returning to a lower elevation to sleep, which stresses the body's adaptation without fully committing to the higher altitude overnight, when breathing naturally slows and oxygen saturation dips further. Once above about 10,000 feet, a widely used guideline is to increase the *sleeping* elevation by no more than roughly 1,000 feet (300m) per night, and to schedule a full rest day — no net elevation gain — every 3 to 4 days, or after every 3,000 feet (roughly 1,000m) of cumulative altitude gained since the last rest day. Physical fitness does not protect against AMS the way people assume it will; a very fit young adult who ascends fast gets it just as often as someone less fit who paces properly, which surprises a lot of strong hikers who assume conditioning is the deciding factor. Alcohol and sedative medications suppress breathing and worsen the body's ability to compensate for low oxygen, so both should be avoided during the acclimatization window, particularly in the first nights spent at any new altitude, even when the day's exertion makes a drink feel earned.

sections.heading: Preventive Medication and When to Consider It
sections.body: Acetazolamide (commonly known by the brand name Diamox) is a preventive medication that speeds up the kidney's natural acclimatization response — the same bicarbonate-excretion process the body performs on its own over several days — essentially giving that process a head start before symptoms have a chance to develop. It's commonly started the day before ascent and continued through the first several days at the target altitude; typical prophylactic dosing is often in the range of 125mg taken twice daily, but the exact dose, timing, and whether it's appropriate at all for a given person's health history should come from a clinician or travel-medicine consult well before the trip, not improvised in the field from something read online. Common, generally harmless side effects include tingling in the fingers and toes, increased urination, and carbonated drinks tasting oddly flat — worth knowing in advance so they aren't mistaken for something more serious. It is a preventive pacing aid that measurably lowers the odds of AMS — it is not a treatment for AMS, HAPE, or HACE symptoms that have already appeared, and taking it does not replace sensible ascent rates, deliberate hydration, or the willingness to turn back if symptoms show up regardless.

sections.heading: Cold and Intense UV: The Altitude Double Exposure
sections.body: High elevation stacks two environmental stresses that are each dangerous alone and considerably worse together. UV radiation intensity increases roughly 10–12% for every 1,000 meters of elevation gained, simply because there's less atmosphere overhead to filter it before it reaches the ground, and fresh snow can reflect back as much as 80% of the UV striking it — meaning exposed skin and eyes take a dose from above and below at the same time, something rarely true at lower elevations. Snow blindness (photokeratitis) is a painful corneal sunburn that can develop within just a few hours of unprotected exposure to bright snow, sometimes not fully felt until hours after the exposure has already happened, and while it typically resolves with dark rest over roughly 24–48 hours, it's genuinely debilitating and can temporarily blind someone in the meantime. At the same time, thin air holds less heat, wind chill is amplified by frequently exposed and windswept terrain, and the drier air combined with the faster breathing altitude demands accelerates fluid loss through respiration alone — compounding both cold-injury risk (see frostbite and hypothermia in the Cold & Hypothermia guide) and dehydration in a way that neither factor produces by itself. Category-appropriate sunglasses or goggles with UV400-rated lenses and side coverage, high-SPF protection for lips and any exposed skin, and proper cold-weather layering are mandatory altitude gear, not optional extras to consider packing if there's room.

sections.heading: Special Populations and Pre-Existing Conditions
sections.body: Altitude illness risk isn't evenly distributed, and a few groups deserve extra caution and, ideally, medical advice before departure. People with pre-existing heart or lung conditions — including asthma, COPD, or heart failure — should get a clinician's input before serious altitude travel, since the extra cardiovascular and respiratory demand of thin air can strain a system that's already compensating for something else. Pregnancy at high altitude is generally considered lower-risk for short visits but warrants an obstetric consult for extended stays or anything above moderate elevation, since maternal oxygen delivery matters for the fetus too. Children can develop AMS just as adults do, but younger children may not reliably describe a headache or nausea, so caregivers should watch instead for unusual fussiness, poor appetite, or lethargy as the practical warning signs, and treat them with the same seriousness as a reported headache in an adult. Anyone with a history of a prior HAPE or HACE episode is at meaningfully elevated risk of it recurring on a future trip and should plan an even more conservative ascent rate, discuss preventive medication with a clinician in advance, and consider having a lower personal threshold for turning back than the rest of the group.

sections.heading: Descent: The One Treatment That Always Works
sections.body: For every form of altitude illness, and especially for HAPE and HACE, descent is the one treatment that reliably works when everything else about the situation is uncertain or the diagnosis isn't perfectly clear. Even a modest drop of 1,000 to 3,300 feet (roughly 300–1,000m) can produce dramatic, sometimes rapid improvement within hours, often faster than any medication alone. A few rules make descent actually effective rather than a near-miss decided too late: never let a symptomatic person descend alone, since impaired judgment and coordination are part of the danger itself, not just a side effect to work around; descend at the first clear sign of HAPE or HACE rather than waiting to see if it passes on its own, since both can deteriorate within a single night; and treat supplemental oxygen and portable hyperbaric bags as tools to stabilize someone for evacuation, not as substitutes for actually losing elevation as soon as it's safely possible. If symptoms fail to improve, or actively worsen, despite a full rest day at the same altitude, that is the clearest possible signal to go down immediately — not to push on and hope acclimatization will somehow catch up overnight.

sections.heading: Practical Checklist for Traveling and Working at Altitude
sections.body: 1) Research the target elevation and plan a realistic ascent rate before departure, not after arriving and discovering the itinerary is too aggressive. 2) Build acclimatization rest days into the itinerary from the start, rather than treating them as optional if time allows. 3) Carry a written personal symptom reference for AMS, HAPE, and HACE so early signs aren't second-guessed or rationalized away in the moment. 4) Pack a pulse oximeter and know each person's normal baseline readings at altitude before assuming a number is abnormal. 5) Hydrate deliberately — thin, dry air increases fluid loss through faster breathing alone, independent of exertion or sweating. 6) Favor a higher-carbohydrate diet at altitude, which the body metabolizes more efficiently under hypoxic conditions than fat or protein. 7) Avoid alcohol and sedatives during the acclimatization window, especially the first nights at any new elevation. 8) Pack UV-rated eye and skin protection as core gear from the packing list, not an afterthought added at the last minute. 9) Know the descent route and evacuation plan before anyone shows symptoms, not after someone is already confused or breathless. 10) Set one firm group rule in advance: anyone showing AMS symptoms does not ascend further that day, no exceptions and no group pressure to keep pace with the itinerary.

guides.title: Humid Tropics & Rainforest Survival
guides.summary: Constant heat, near-total humidity, and dense biological life turn the tropics into their own survival discipline — one where staying dry matters just as much as staying cool.

sections.heading: A Different Kind of Heat
sections.body: Tropical rainforest heat rarely reaches the extreme air temperatures a dry desert can produce — daytime highs typically sit in the 85–100°F (29–38°C) range rather than pushing past 115°F — but it makes up for that with relentless, near-total humidity, often 80–100% relative humidity around the clock, day and night alike. A dry desert climate usually drops sharply after sunset, giving the body a genuine overnight recovery window to shed accumulated heat strain; tropical nights often stay warm and just as humid as the day, denying that recovery period entirely. Dense canopy cover and near-daily rainfall don't relieve the heat the way a passing shower might elsewhere — falling rain often raises humidity further as it evaporates off saturated vegetation and standing water rather than cooling the air meaningfully. The combined effect of sustained heat, sustained humidity, and no overnight relief is, over multiple days, often more physiologically taxing on the body than a hotter but drier and cooler-at-night desert climate, even though the peak thermometer reading looks less dramatic. This is the core reason tropical heat management deserves its own approach rather than simply applying desert-heat rules with a humidity footnote.

sections.heading: Why Sweat Stops Working
sections.body: Evaporative cooling — the body's primary defense against overheating — depends on a vapor-pressure gradient between wet skin and the surrounding air; sweat only cools effectively as it evaporates, not simply by being produced. Once relative humidity climbs above roughly 75–80%, the surrounding air is already close to saturated with water vapor and can accept very little more, so sweat increasingly beads and drips off the skin instead of evaporating — the body keeps losing fluid and electrolytes without gaining the cooling benefit that fluid loss is supposed to buy. Core body temperature can keep climbing even while a person is visibly drenched and clearly sweating heavily, which is counterintuitive and catches people off guard because "I'm sweating a lot" normally reads as a sign the cooling system is working. Wet-bulb temperature — a single measurement that accounts for both heat and humidity together, discussed in more depth in the Heat & Desert guide — is a far better predictor of real danger in the tropics than the plain thermometer reading. The practical response is to rest deliberately through the hottest, most humid stretch of the day, actively seek out air movement since shade with a breeze cools far better than still shade alone, and never assume "I don't feel that hot" is reliable — humid heat illness can advance with noticeably less warning than dry desert heat does.

sections.heading: Recognizing Heat Illness Faster in Humid Conditions
sections.body: Because sweat's cooling effect is blunted by humidity, heat exhaustion and heat stroke can progress with less obvious warning in the tropics than in a dry climate, and the window between "uncomfortable" and "dangerous" can be shorter than expected. Watch for heavy sweating that doesn't seem to actually cool the person, muscle cramping, headache, nausea, and general weakness — the pattern of heat exhaustion, which calls for rest, shade, fluids, and active cooling. Hot, sometimes still-wet skin combined with confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination, or collapse signals heat stroke, a true medical emergency requiring aggressive cooling — wet cloths paired with active fanning or forced air movement, deep shade, and ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin if available — plus urgent evacuation. In humid conditions, active air movement matters more than it does in dry heat, because it's often the only practical way to get any evaporation happening at all when the surrounding air is already saturated; a hand fan, walking deliberately into whatever breeze exists, or fanning with a broad leaf are not minor comfort measures here, they're genuine first-line treatment tools.

sections.heading: Jungle Rot and Fungal Skin Breakdown
sections.body: "Jungle rot" is the long-standing field term for skin that stays wet for days on end — soaked by sweat, rain, and river crossings with no real chance to dry out — and gradually breaks down into fungal infections (tinea, similar in cause to athlete's foot but able to spread to the groin, underarms, and other skin folds), secondary bacterial infections, and macerated, cracking skin, especially between the toes and in any place where skin touches skin. Left untreated, it can ulcerate and become a genuine wound-infection risk in a climate already dense with bacteria and biting insects looking for exactly that kind of opening. Prevention centers on drying feet and skin whenever any opportunity arises: change socks when they get wet rather than waiting for camp, air out boots at every rest stop, and use antifungal or plain foot powder proactively rather than only after symptoms appear. Avoid staying in soaked clothing overnight even when it's inconvenient to change. Treat early fungal patches — itchy, red, ring-shaped patches, or pale, soggy-looking skin — with antifungal cream and, just as importantly, by keeping the area genuinely dry going forward. A daily skin-fold check, done the same way a tick check is done elsewhere, catches problems while they're still minor and easy to manage.

sections.heading: Camp Craft for a Climate That Never Dries Out
sections.body: Sleeping off the ground — a hammock with a rain tarp strung above and a bug net below — keeps a person clear of ground moisture, runoff, and crawling insects far better than a ground tent does across most rainforest terrain, and it's the standard approach for good reason. Everything mildews eventually in this climate: pack genuinely critical items such as matches, documents, and electronics in truly waterproof containers or properly sealed dry bags, not merely "water-resistant" gear, and take advantage of any dry spell to open and air everything out. Fire is noticeably harder to start and sustain in constant humidity than in a temperate climate — split wood to expose its drier interior, build a raised platform to keep the fire base off damp ground, and keep a dedicated, protected reserve of dry tinder that never gets touched except when genuinely needed. Launder and dry clothing at every real opportunity, even if it means wearing a damp backup item for a few hours in the meantime — clothing that stays perpetually wet is both a surprising hypothermia risk (yes, even in the tropics, particularly overnight or at any elevation) and a direct driver of the skin problems described above.

sections.heading: Monsoon and Wet-Season Hazards
sections.body: Seasonal monsoon rain in tropical regions can dump extreme totals of rainfall in just a few hours, and dense jungle terrain concentrates that water efficiently into flash floods along stream beds and low ground with very little advance warning — a completely dry creek bed can turn into a dangerous torrent within minutes from rain falling miles away and upstream, long before any rain is visible or falling overhead. Never camp in a dry wash or streambed during the wet season, regardless of how flat, clear, or convenient it looks compared to the surrounding terrain. River crossings that were straightforward in the dry season can become impassable or genuinely lethal once the wet season sets in; if a crossing looks fast, looks deep, or is visibly rising while being assessed, the correct move is to wait it out or find an alternate route rather than attempt to push across. Lightning is also a serious hazard during monsoon-season storms in open or elevated terrain within the forest; during a storm, seek lower, non-exposed ground well away from the tallest trees in the immediate area, following the same general lightning-safety principles that apply anywhere else.

sections.heading: Living With Insect and Parasite Density
sections.body: The tropics carry a far higher density of disease-carrying insects than most temperate climates, and the practical risk is proportionally higher too: mosquitoes (carrying malaria, dengue, Zika, or yellow fever depending on the specific region), ticks and mites — including chiggers that transmit scrub typhus across parts of Asia and the Pacific — and leeches in wet ground and streams. A workable layered defense includes permethrin-treated clothing, which kills or repels insects on contact and survives many wash cycles; DEET or picaridin applied to exposed skin; sleeping under a permethrin-treated bug net even inside a hammock setup; tucking pant legs into socks or boot tops; and a nightly full-body check specifically for ticks and leeches. A leech is best removed by sliding a fingernail or a flat edge under its sucker to break the seal rather than pulling it straight off, which can leave mouthparts embedded and increase infection risk. Any fever, chills, or unusual rash appearing days to weeks after a bite in a tropical region should be treated seriously as a possible mosquito- or tick-borne illness and evaluated by a medical professional, not dismissed as an ordinary flu that will pass on its own.

sections.heading: Finding and Purifying Water Under Canopy
sections.body: Water is rarely scarce in rainforest terrain the way it is in a desert, but it is almost always biologically contaminated — even clear-looking jungle streams routinely carry bacteria, protozoa such as Giardia, and viruses introduced by upstream animal and human activity, so appearance is not a useful indicator of safety here. Collect from moving water where possible rather than stagnant pools, and always treat what's collected: boiling for one full minute at low elevation (extending to three minutes above roughly 6,500 feet/2,000m) reliably kills essentially all biological hazards, or use a rated filter with an absolute pore size of 0.2 micron or smaller, ideally combined with a chemical treatment or UV step to address viruses that a filter alone may not reliably catch. Some thick, woody vines (cut low, then high, to release trapped water they carry) and certain palm species can yield genuinely drinkable water in an emergency, but this is a specialized, last-resort skill that requires accurate species identification specific to the region — it should never be treated as a primary water strategy or a general "jungle vines have water" assumption applied indiscriminately.

sections.heading: Orientation and Shelter Under Dense Canopy
sections.body: Dense canopy blocks sky-based navigation cues — sun position, stars — for much of the day, and thick understory can limit visibility to just a few meters in places, making it genuinely easy to lose a clear sense of direction faster than most people expect from open terrain. A compass or GPS becomes far more important here than in open country, and deliberately marking a path as it's traveled — blazes, flagging tape, or small cairns placed at regular intervals — is well worth the extra time it costs. Sound and light behave differently under canopy too: the forest floor is often quieter than the canopy itself, where wind and animal activity concentrate, so listening carefully for the sound of moving water — a reliable and consistent navigation and resource handrail — is frequently more useful than listening for other ambient cues. Choose camp sites on slightly elevated, well-drained ground, away from any obviously dead "widow-maker" branches or trees overhead — falling limbs, not predators, are a leading and underappreciated cause of injury in rainforest camps, particularly during or after wind and rain.

sections.heading: Soil- and Water-Borne Disease Risks Beyond Insect Bites
sections.body: Insects aren't the only tropical disease vector worth planning around — soil and freshwater carry their own risks that have nothing to do with bites or stings. Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection picked up from water or mud contaminated with the urine of infected animals (rodents especially), entering through small cuts, scrapes, or mucous membranes like the eyes, nose, or mouth during river crossings, flooding, or simply wading through standing water; symptoms mimic flu at first — fever, headache, muscle aches — which makes it easy to dismiss until it progresses. Hookworm larvae live in soil contaminated by infected feces and can penetrate bare or thinly protected skin, most often through the soles of the feet, which is the core reason footwear should stay on even around camp rather than going barefoot for comfort. In parts of Africa, Asia, and South America, schistosomiasis is transmitted by freshwater snails living in slow-moving streams, lakes, and irrigation channels, entering through skin contact with infested water — a genuine reason to research regional water hazards before swimming or wading in unfamiliar freshwater, not just before drinking it. None of these require constant fear, but they do argue for keeping footwear on around camp, covering open cuts before water contact, avoiding submersion of the face and mucous membranes in untreated freshwater, and treating any unexplained fever that develops after the trip as worth mentioning to a doctor along with the travel history.

sections.heading: Tropical Field Checklist
sections.body: 1) Sleep off the ground under a permethrin-treated bug net with a rain cover overhead rather than in a ground tent where practical. 2) Pack genuinely critical items in truly waterproof containers, not merely water-resistant ones. 3) Treat all water before drinking regardless of how clear it looks. 4) Dry feet and skin whenever possible and treat any fungal patches the moment they appear rather than waiting. 5) Wear permethrin-treated clothing and apply DEET or picaridin to exposed skin consistently, not just when insects are already biting. 6) Never camp in a dry wash or streambed during wet season no matter how convenient it looks. 7) Rest deliberately through the hottest, most humid part of the day and actively seek moving air rather than still shade. 8) Carry a compass or GPS for under-canopy navigation and mark the route as it's traveled. 9) Inspect for ticks and leeches every night as a fixed camp routine. 10) Treat any fever or unusual rash appearing after time in the tropics as a possible tropical illness and seek medical evaluation promptly rather than waiting it out.

guides.title: Coastal & Maritime Climate Hazards
guides.summary: Living or traveling near open water brings its own hazard set — storm surge, rip currents, and salt air that quietly destroys anything metal — distinct from the weather itself.

sections.heading: Why the Coast Is a Distinct Hazard Zone
sections.body: Coastal and maritime environments combine several hazards that simply don't exist, or exist in much milder form, farther inland. Storms that form or pass over warm ocean water draw energy from it and can intensify dramatically in the final day or two before landfall, arriving stronger than they left port. The ocean itself introduces water-driven hazards inland communities never plan for — storm surge, rip currents, and tsunamis — on top of whatever the storm's winds and rain are doing. Airborne salt corrodes metal, electronics, and infrastructure far faster than an equivalent inland climate, a slow background hazard that's easy to ignore until a critical piece of gear fails at the wrong moment. And coastal geography often concentrates evacuation routes onto a small number of bridges, causeways, or coastal highways, so the infrastructure that gets a population out of harm's way is frequently the same infrastructure most vulnerable to flooding and wind damage. Coastal climates also tend to be more humid and see more frequent, sudden weather changes than inland areas at the same latitude, since the ocean itself moderates temperature but also feeds moisture into every passing system. None of these hazards are exotic or rare — they're a predictable, recurring part of living or operating near open water, and treating the coast as "inland weather plus a nice view" is the most common preparedness mistake.

sections.heading: Storm Surge: The Deadliest Part of a Hurricane
sections.body: Storm surge is the abnormal rise of ocean water pushed ashore by a storm's wind and low central pressure, and historically it has been the deadliest single hazard in hurricanes and typhoons — many of the most catastrophic death tolls from storms like Hurricane Katrina and Typhoon Haiyan came primarily from surge, not from wind. Two mechanisms combine to produce it: sustained onshore wind literally piles ocean water toward the coastline ahead of the storm, and the storm's unusually low central pressure allows the sea surface beneath it to dome upward slightly, a secondary effect roughly on the order of an inch of rise for every millibar of pressure drop, smaller than the wind-driven piling but still meaningful. Surge height depends heavily on storm intensity, physical size, forward speed, angle of approach relative to the coastline, and critically the shape of the seafloor near shore — shallow, gently sloping continental shelves, like much of the U.S. Gulf Coast, produce dramatically higher surge than steep coastlines where deep water sits close to land. Surge can arrive hours before the storm's strongest winds and can continue pushing seawater miles inland along rivers and low-lying ground well after the wind has died down. This is exactly why storm surge risk is mapped and graded separately from wind category, and why evacuation orders are based on surge-risk maps rather than the wind-speed category alone.

sections.heading: Hurricane/Typhoon Categories and Preparedness Timelines
sections.body: The Saffir-Simpson scale grades hurricanes by sustained wind speed alone: Category 1 runs 74–95 mph, Category 2 is 96–110 mph, Category 3 (the threshold for "major") is 111–129 mph, Category 4 is 130–156 mph, and Category 5 is 157 mph and above — but the scale says nothing directly about rainfall or storm surge, which is why a "weaker" storm by category can still be catastrophic through flooding alone. A hurricane or tropical storm watch means conditions are possible within roughly 48 hours and it's time to finish preparations that haven't been started yet; a warning means conditions are expected within roughly 36 hours and it's time to complete final preparations or evacuate if ordered, not begin planning from scratch. A workable prep timeline looks like: around 5 days out, monitor forecasts closely and review supplies against the household plan; around 3 days out, fuel every vehicle, secure important documents, and fill water containers and bathtubs; when a watch is issued, secure or bring in loose outdoor items and confirm the evacuation route if the property sits in a surge zone; once a warning is issued, complete any ordered evacuation promptly, since leaving after winds have already picked up is measurably more dangerous than leaving early. Waiting to decide until conditions are already visibly bad removes the safest option from the table.

sections.heading: Rip Currents: The Everyday Coastal Killer
sections.body: Rip currents are narrow, powerful channels of water flowing away from shore, formed where incoming waves push water toward the beach and it funnels back out to sea through a gap in a sandbar or near a structure like a jetty or pier — and unlike hurricanes, they're a routine hazard on ordinary sunny beach days, responsible for the majority of beach lifeguard rescues in many coastal areas. They commonly move at 1–2 feet per second and can reach roughly 8 feet per second (around 5–8 mph) in strong cases — faster than most swimmers, including strong ones, can swim directly against. Signs visible from shore include a channel of choppier, discolored, or foamy water moving steadily out to sea, and a noticeable gap or break in the otherwise regular incoming wave line. If caught in one, the correct response is to not fight it by swimming straight back toward shore — instead, swim parallel to the beach until clear of the current's pull, then angle back in once free of it; if escape isn't possible, floating or treading water and signaling for help is the safer choice, since most rip currents weaken and dissipate a relatively short distance offshore rather than pulling a swimmer out indefinitely. Most rip-current drownings result from panic and exhaustion spent fighting the current head-on, not from the current's raw strength alone.

sections.heading: Salt-Air Corrosion: Keeping Gear Alive
sections.body: Airborne salt — sea spray aerosolized by wave action, which can travel a mile or more inland on a steady onshore wind — accelerates the corrosion of anything metal far faster than an equivalent inland environment; galvanized fasteners, firearms, hand tools, electronics contacts, vehicle undercarriages, and bicycle chains can show significant corrosion within weeks in a coastal setting where an inland equivalent might take years to reach the same state. Practical countermeasures make a real difference: rinse any gear that's been exposed to spray with fresh water and dry it thoroughly afterward rather than letting salt residue sit; favor marine-grade stainless steel, anodized aluminum, or specifically coated fasteners for anything stored or used outdoors; keep silica gel packets or a small dehumidifier running in storage lockers, cabinets, or gun safes; apply a light oil or a corrosion-inhibiting spray formulated for marine hardware on exposed metal surfaces periodically; and inspect electrical connections and battery terminals more frequently than the manufacturer's inland-rated maintenance schedule suggests, since salt-driven corrosion there tends to cause quiet, gradual failures rather than obvious visible damage until something stops working entirely. Firearms and edged tools kept in a coastal home benefit from a light coat of corrosion-inhibiting oil even in storage, not only after active use, since the ambient salt content of the air itself is enough to start pitting bare steel over time without any direct spray contact at all.

sections.heading: Tsunami: Reading Nature's Own Warning
sections.body: Tsunamis are usually triggered by undersea earthquakes, though landslides and volcanic activity can also generate them, and they can arrive with little or no official warning at all when the triggering event happens close to shore, leaving no time for a broadcast alert to matter. There are natural warning signs worth acting on immediately, without waiting for a siren or official notification: a strong or unusually long-lasting earthquake felt near the coast, the ocean visibly and rapidly receding far beyond the normal low-tide line, or a loud, unusual roaring sound coming from the water. Any single one of these signs is reason enough to move immediately toward high ground — generally advised to be at least 100 feet (30m) in elevation — or at minimum a couple of miles inland, on foot if roads are jammed with traffic, without pausing to wait and see what develops next. The first wave in a tsunami sequence is frequently not the largest, and tsunamis typically arrive as a series of waves spread out over an hour or more, so returning to the coastline after the first wave passes is a documented cause of additional casualties. Coastal communities in known tsunami-risk zones, particularly around the Pacific, often maintain siren networks and posted evacuation-route signage — learning that signage and the nearest high ground before it's needed costs nothing and can save the minutes that matter most.

sections.heading: Evacuation Zones and Planning
sections.body: Most coastal areas prone to storm surge or tsunami risk publish evacuation zone maps — often lettered A/B/C or numbered by tier — tied to storm category or expected surge height, and the time to learn a specific zone assignment is before hurricane season begins, not while a storm is already approaching. A workable evacuation plan includes a specific inland destination along with at least two possible route options, since bridges and causeways can become single points of failure and are often closed earliest as conditions deteriorate; a full fuel tank and some cash on hand well before roads and gas stations get crowded; a copy of important documents kept in a waterproof bag ready to grab; and a concrete plan for pets and anyone with mobility needs, since public shelters and organized evacuation transport don't automatically accommodate either without advance arrangement. The single most useful habit is leaving earlier than feels strictly necessary — evacuation traffic during a mandated coastal evacuation routinely turns what would normally be a two-hour drive into eight, twelve, or more hours once everyone on the coast tries to leave through the same limited set of roads at once.

sections.heading: After the Storm: The Hazards That Outlast the Wind
sections.body: Coastal disaster hazards continue well past the point where the storm itself has passed and the sky has cleared. Floodwater can be contaminated with sewage, fuel, and various chemicals and should be treated as unsafe to wade through or drink without purification, regardless of how it looks. Downed power lines may remain energized and are especially dangerous where they've come into contact with standing water, which can conduct current well beyond the visible line itself. Structural damage — an undermined foundation, a weakened roof, compromised load-bearing walls — may not be visible just from looking at a building's exterior, so re-entering a damaged structure deserves real caution rather than assuming "it's still standing, so it's fine." Carbon monoxide poisoning from generators run too close to living spaces is a leading cause of death in the days immediately following a coastal storm; run generators at least 20 feet from any window or door, and never inside a garage even with the door left open. Boil-water advisories are common after coastal flooding because storm surge and heavy rain can overwhelm municipal water treatment systems, so tap water should be treated as unsafe to drink until an advisory is officially and explicitly lifted.

sections.heading: Small-Craft and Boating Safety in Coastal Weather
sections.body: Coastal weather can shift from manageable to dangerous for a small boat far faster than it does for someone on land, and marine conditions deserve their own forecast check, not an assumption that the land forecast covers it. Marine weather forecasts and small-craft advisories exist specifically because wind that feels unremarkable on shore can generate steep, closely-spaced waves offshore that a small vessel handles very differently than open water conditions the forecast's general wind number would suggest; a small-craft advisory typically means sustained winds or waves have crossed a threshold considered hazardous for smaller recreational boats, and it should be treated as a real decision point about whether to go out at all, not a minor caveat. Sudden squalls, common along many coastlines especially in warmer months, can arrive with little warning and produce a rapid spike in wind and wave height well ahead of any visible storm cell reaching the boat's position. Cold water immersion is a serious risk even along otherwise warm coastlines, since water temperature drops with depth and season far more than air temperature does, and a capsizing that seems survivable based on air temperature alone can turn into a genuine hypothermia emergency in the water within a much shorter window than expected. A properly worn life jacket — not just one stowed aboard — a filed float plan telling someone ashore the route and expected return time, and a habit of checking the marine forecast specifically before departure are the three simplest changes that prevent the largest share of small-craft coastal emergencies.

sections.heading: Coastal Preparedness Checklist
sections.body: 1) Know the property's surge or tsunami evacuation zone and a planned inland route before hurricane season starts, not once a storm is already forecast. 2) Treat a hurricane watch, not just a warning, as the moment to act — a watch means roughly 48 hours, a warning means roughly 36. 3) Rinse and dry salt-exposed gear on a regular schedule, and store critical metal items with desiccant to slow corrosion. 4) Never swim near a visibly identifiable rip current channel, and know the parallel-swim escape technique before it's needed. 5) Treat any sudden, unusual ocean recession or a strong coastal earthquake as an immediate tsunami warning requiring movement to high ground, with no waiting for confirmation. 6) Keep fuel tanks topped off and important documents packed in a waterproof bag as a standing habit throughout hurricane season, not a last-minute task. 7) Run generators outdoors and well away from windows and doors after any storm, never in an enclosed or semi-enclosed space. 8) Treat all floodwater and tap water as contaminated until officially confirmed safe. 9) Evacuate early — traffic congestion, not the storm itself, is very often the real time constraint that determines whether an evacuation succeeds.

guides.title: Arid Climate & Long-Term Drought Adaptation
guides.summary: Surviving one brutal desert day is one skill; living for months or years where water is chronically scarce is another — this is the long game of budgeting, sourcing, and adapting to dry country.

sections.heading: Acute Desert Heat vs. Long-Term Arid Living
sections.body: The Heat & Desert guide covers the acute emergency — extreme heat, immediate hydration needs, getting rescued before heat stroke sets in. This guide covers a different problem entirely: sustained, ongoing life in a climate where water is chronically scarce, not just dangerously hot for a day or two.
